adjudication_records.issue_text: junit and hamcrest dependencies added in authz/client/pom.xml have no version and no dependencyManagement entry, risking build failure if the parent chain does not manage them

adjudication.rationale: In authz/client/pom.xml the newly added test dependencies for `junit:junit` and `org.hamcrest:hamcrest` do not specify `<version>`. This is only valid if versions are provided via a parent POM/BOM `<dependencyManagement>`, which is not shown in this diff; otherwise Maven resolution will fail. The finding’s conditional warning about build risk is therefore diff-grounded but not fully verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of KeyStore.getDefaultType() (the JDK file KeyStore provider) instead of BouncyCastle, causing NoSuchAlgorithmException for callers expecting BC-specific algorithms

All three server-side CryptoProviders (default, elytron, fips1402) return order() == 200, so tie-breaking falls to ServiceLoader iteration order, which can silently pick a non-FIPS provider in FIPS setups where both jars are present

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to sort providers by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and then silently choose foundProviders.get(0), only logging others instead of failing when multiple are present. In the same diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all implement order() returning 200, so when more than one of these jars is on the classpath they tie and selection falls back to ServiceLoader encounter order (stable sort preserves iteration order). This can result in an unintended provider being picked (e.g., non-FIPS when FIPS is also present), which is a real behavior/security defect exposed by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Fail-fast guarantee for conflicting crypto providers silently removed: equal-order tie (both DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider return order() == 200) falls back to arbitrary ServiceLoader iteration order, nondeterministically picking a provider with only a debug log

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the previous fail-fast when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found (CryptoIntegration.detectProvider no longer throws when foundProviders.size() > 1) and instead sorts only by CryptoProvider::order descending and picks foundProviders.get(0), logging the rest at debug. In this same diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return the same order() == 200, so ties are not broken deterministically by the comparator. With equal orders, the selected provider depends on the underlying ServiceLoader iteration order, making provider selection ambiguous/non-deterministic and no longer enforced as an error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test anywhere in the diff exercises the multi-provider or equal-order tie case

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes provider selection semantics in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` by sorting all `CryptoProvider`s by `order()` descending and picking the first, while logging the rest (instead of throwing when `foundProviders.size() > 1`). This introduces nontrivial behavior for multi-provider and equal-order ties (`.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`), but the only added test (`authz/client/src/test/.../ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java`) exercises ECDSA signature encoding/decoding and does not cover multiple providers on the classpath or equal `order()` tie behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: int order() added to CryptoProvider SPI as abstract method with no default implementation, breaking binary and source compatibility for third-party implementations (compile error or AbstractMethodError at runtime)

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new abstract method `int order();` to the public SPI interface `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` (common/src/main/java/.../CryptoProvider.java) without a default implementation. That is a breaking change for any existing third-party `CryptoProvider` implementations: source incompatibility (won’t compile until they implement `order()`), and binary incompatibility (older compiled implementations would fail at runtime when the method is invoked, typically via `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` now sorting by `CryptoProvider::order`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements only 2 of ~20 CryptoProvider methods, rest throw UnsupportedOperationException, with no stated/tested contract for which subset is supported; real authz-client flows like truststore handling and token signature verification hit throwing methods at runtime

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new service-loaded CryptoProvider (META-INF/services/... -> AuthzClientCryptoProvider) and makes AuthzClient.create() call CryptoIntegration.init(...), which will auto-detect and use the highest-order provider available. AuthzClientCryptoProvider only meaningfully implements a small subset (getBouncyCastleProvider, order, getEcdsaCryptoProvider, getKeyStore) and leaves most of the CryptoProvider contract throwing UnsupportedOperationException. The finding’s claim that it implements “only 2” methods is inaccurate, and the diff does not show any concrete authz-client flow calling the unsupported methods, so a definite runtime bug can’t be verified from the diff alone. However, registering a partially-implemented provider is a real, diff-grounded risk/contract issue because any shared code path that uses other CryptoProvider methods would now fail at runtime when this provider is the only/selected one.

adjudication_records.issue_text: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK default KeyStore provider (SUN) instead of BouncyCastle, causing callers requesting BC algorithms to get NoSuchAlgorithmException
matched_golden_ids: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the method intended to return the BouncyCastle provider instead returns the default JDK keystore/provider (e.g., SUN), leading to failures when BC-specific algorithms are requested.

matched_golden_ids: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags dead code where ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) is invoked but the result is discarded, matching the golden issue that earlier encoder instances are unused because subsequent new encoders perform the actual return encoding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ECDSAAlgorithmTest round-trip assertion never verifies against original JDK-produced sign bytes nor validates DER output via Signature.verify, so a self-consistent but broken encoding would pass the test

adjudication.rationale: In `ECDSAAlgorithmTest`, the test flow is `sign (JDK DER) -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS` and it only asserts `rsConcat` equals `rsConcat2`. It never checks that the re-encoded DER (`asn1Des`) matches the original JDK-produced `sign` bytes, nor does it call `Signature.verify` on `asn1Des`. Therefore, an implementation where the decoder/encoder are mutually consistent but not actually producing JCA-valid DER (or not preserving canonical DER) could still pass this test. This is a test coverage/validation gap, not a verifiable production defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Scope drift: silent removal of the multiple-provider IllegalStateException hard failure in CryptoIntegration, unrelated to the stated PR intent — server admins with duplicate providers now get silent order()-based selection with only DEBUG-level logging instead of a loud startup failure

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(): it no longer throws an IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found. Instead it sorts by CryptoProvider::order (reversed) and returns the first, logging only at DEBUG level that others were ignored (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral change (startup hard-fail -> silent selection), but it’s not inherently a correctness defect on its own given the newly introduced order() mechanism in CryptoProvider and implementations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unnecessary implementation work spread across three server-side crypto modules (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) to support a client-only provider

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `CryptoProvider` gained a new required method `order()` and `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` now sorts providers by this order instead of throwing when multiple are present. As a result, existing provider implementations (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`) must implement `order()` to compile and to participate in selection. While a new client-side provider (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `order()=100`) was added, the claim that the server-side changes are “unnecessary implementation work … to support a client-only provider” is subjective and not verifiable from the diff; the changes are mechanically required by the interface change and apply generally to all providers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: order() values (200 vs 100) are hidden coupling: hand-maintained magic numbers with no single point defining the ranking and no collision handling — two providers returning the same order fall back to nondeterministic ServiceLoader order

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new priority mechanism via `CryptoProvider.order()` and changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(...)` to select the highest `order()` by sorting providers descending. The concrete implementations added/updated hard-code values (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() == 100`, others `== 200`) with no shared definition, which is a form of hidden coupling. Also, there is no explicit tie-breaker for equal `order()` values; selection would then depend on the encounter order from `ServiceLoader.load(...)` after sorting, which is not explicitly made deterministic in this code (no secondary sort key / collision handling). This is a maintainability/architecture concern rather than a directly verifiable functional defect in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: order() added as a breaking interface change to CryptoProvider — adding an abstract method breaks every existing third-party implementation; a default method would have satisfied the need without breakage

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new abstract method `int order()` to the `CryptoProvider` interface (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java). This is a source/binary incompatible API change for any existing external/third-party implementations of `CryptoProvider` not updated in this repo. While in-repo implementations were updated (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and the new AuthzClientCryptoProvider), the interface change itself is still a concrete compatibility concern; making it a `default` method could have avoided breaking external implementers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Under-scoping: AuthzClientCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException for 13 of ~20 CryptoProvider methods yet is registered as a global service via META-INF/services, so any process-global CryptoIntegration caller gets the stub

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` that implements `CryptoProvider` but leaves most methods throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` (e.g., `getPemUtils`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getSignature`, ciphers, key factories, etc.), and registers it via `authz/client/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`. The same PR also makes `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` call `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, which globally selects a provider via `ServiceLoader`. If this authz-client jar is on the classpath without another higher-`order()` provider, `CryptoIntegration` will select this partial provider and any later call to an unsupported method will fail at runtime. The finding’s broad claim about “any process-global caller gets the stub” is somewhat overstated because `CryptoIntegration` now sorts by `order()` and other providers in the diff return `200` vs `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`’s `100`, but the under-scoping risk is real when no other provider is present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER: two ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to but their results are discarded entirely

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create encoders, write to them, and then discard them without using `toByteArray()` or feeding them into the returned sequence. The returned value is built from a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger))`. This is verifiably redundant/dead code (wasted allocations/confusing), but it does not change behavior of the returned encoding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test dependencies (junit, hamcrest) added but tests only cover the isolated conversion helper — CryptoIntegration.init path, service-file selection, and order()-based selection added in this PR ship untested

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new nontrivial runtime-selection behavior that is not exercised by the added tests. Specifically: (1) `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, which changes initialization behavior but has no test coverage. (2) `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(...)` was changed to sort `ServiceLoader` results by the new `CryptoProvider::order` (descending) and to ignore additional providers instead of throwing; a new `order()` method was added to the `CryptoProvider` interface and implemented across providers. (3) A new SPI file `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` is added for `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`. The only new test (`ECDSAAlgorithmTest`) validates ECDSA signature conversion helpers in isolation and does not cover the init path, SPI discovery, or order-based provider selection behavior introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Multi-provider resolution in CryptoIntegration.java silently picks one provider instead of failing fast, allowing a FIPS deployment to silently run non-FIPS crypto with only a DEBUG-level log

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to no longer fail when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are present. Instead it sorts by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first provider, logging “Ignored crypto providers” only at DEBUG (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). Since multiple built-in providers now all report the same order (200 in DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider), the chosen provider among ties is effectively dependent on ServiceLoader iteration order, meaning a FIPS deployment with multiple providers on the classpath could silently select a non-FIPS provider rather than failing fast.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Provider ties (order()==200 for FIPS1402Provider, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider) are broken by ServiceLoader/classpath order, so the effective provider can flip between identical builds

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() to sort discovered CryptoProvider implementations by order() descending and then select foundProviders.get(0), no longer failing when multiple providers exist. However, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return the same order() value (200). With equal comparator keys, the selected provider depends on the remaining ServiceLoader iteration/encounter order (classpath/service registration order), which is not controlled by this code. Therefore the effective provider can vary when multiple equal-order providers are present, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AuthzClient.create() mutates the process-global static CryptoIntegration provider by re-calling CryptoIntegration.init(), swapping the global provider mid-flight for unrelated code

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader());` inside `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` (authz/client/.../AuthzClient.java). `CryptoIntegration` is a static integration point (see `CryptoIntegration.getProvider()` / `detectProvider(...)` changes in common module), so initializing it from a client factory method introduces a process-wide/global side effect tied to AuthzClient construction. The finding’s stronger claim about “re-calling … swapping the global provider mid-flight” can’t be fully verified from this diff alone (we don’t see `init()`’s idempotence/guards), but the new code does create a real global-state/architecture concern grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements the full CryptoProvider SPI but ~15 of ~20 methods throw UnsupportedOperationException with no compile-time or startup-time signal

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements CryptoProvider` but most SPI methods (e.g., `getAlgorithmProvider`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getPemUtils`, `getKeyPairGen`, `getKeyFactory`, `getAesCbcCipher`, `getSignature`, etc.) unconditionally throw `UnsupportedOperationException` (new file `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java`). Since `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(...)`, this provider can be selected via `ServiceLoader` (see new META-INF/services entry). There is no compile-time or startup-time validation that unimplemented methods won’t be used, so any call into these methods will fail at runtime; however, the diff alone doesn’t prove those methods are exercised in normal authz-client flows, so it’s a concrete design/runtime-risk issue rather than a verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default JKS/PKCS12 keystore provider instead of BouncyCastle, misleading callers expecting BC semantics

adjudication.rationale: In the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()` (i.e., the provider of the platform default keystore type, typically a Sun* provider), not a BouncyCastle provider. This contradicts the `CryptoProvider` interface contract/comment added/used in this diff (“Get bouncycastle security provider...”), and can mislead/break callers that rely on BC-specific provider semantics when this provider is selected via `ServiceLoader` (notably in an authz-client-only classpath where it may be the only provider).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unconditional registration of the stub AuthzClientCryptoProvider in META-INF/services in the authz-client jar converts a loud startup failure into a deferred runtime failure for mis-assembled classpaths

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a service provider entry `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` pointing to `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, and `AuthzClient.create(...)` now unconditionally calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`. `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` is largely a stub (many methods throw `UnsupportedOperationException`), but its presence means `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(...)` will now successfully find *a* provider even when the intended crypto modules are missing, rather than failing fast with `IllegalStateException` for “no providers”. That matches the finding that mis-assembled classpaths may defer failure until an unsupported crypto operation is invoked.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ASN1Decoder.readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length (0x80) BER sequences, causing readSequence() to return an empty list instead of rejecting the malformed encoding

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ASN1Decoder`, `readLength()` explicitly returns `-1` for the BER indefinite-length marker (`0x80`). In `readSequence()`, the loop is `while (length > 0)`, so a `-1` length will skip parsing and return an empty `List<byte[]>` without throwing, effectively not rejecting an unsupported/malformed (for DER) encoding at this layer. This behavior is directly verifiable from `ASN1Decoder.readLength()` and `ASN1Decoder.readSequence()` in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Dead allocations in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.concatenatedRSToASN1DER: two ASN1Encoder instances are created and discarded with output never used

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` each create an ASN1Encoder and write into it, but the resulting encoder/bytes are never used. The method then correctly returns a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)).toByteArray();`. This is a real, diff-grounded inefficiency/dead allocation, but it does not change correctness because the returned value comes from the later encoder.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The PR silently deletes the server-wide multiple-CryptoProvider guard in CryptoIntegration.java, replacing a fail-fast IllegalStateException with silent order-based selection that can pick the wrong provider (e.g., non-FIPS) with no error

adjudication.rationale: The diff in CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() removes the previous fail-fast check that threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was loaded, and instead sorts providers by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first while only logging “Ignored crypto providers” at debug. This is a behavior change that can silently select a provider when multiple are present. Additionally, the existing providers in the diff (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) all return the same order() value (200), so when multiple are on the classpath selection can become effectively dependent on ServiceLoader iteration order, making “wrong provider” selection plausible with no error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: All three existing crypto providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) hardcode order() == 200, so the new order-based selection mechanism cannot discriminate between them and mixed-classpath deployments resolve non-deterministically by ServiceLoader order

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to no longer throw when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found; it now sorts by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first provider. However, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all implement order() returning 200 in this diff, so the sort cannot break ties. With multiple of these on the classpath, selection falls back to ServiceLoader iteration order, which is not guaranteed to be consistent, and the code will silently pick one provider and ignore the rest (only logging debug). This can lead to incorrect/non-deterministic provider choice compared to the previous fail-fast behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AuthzClient.create() calls CryptoIntegration.init() with the authz-client classloader on every invocation, re-initializing the JVM-wide active CryptoProvider and silently swapping out a provider (e.g., FIPS) that the rest of the application had already initialized against a different classloader

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now unconditionally calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` on every invocation. `CryptoIntegration` is a static integration point (it has static detection logic) and was changed to (a) sort providers by `CryptoProvider::order` and (b) no longer fail when multiple providers are visible, instead selecting the first and only logging “Ignored crypto providers”. From the diff alone we can’t verify that `init()` actually re-initializes/overwrites a JVM-wide active provider (its implementation isn’t shown), but the change clearly introduces a new global-initialization side effect from a library entrypoint and makes provider selection more silent when multiple are present, which is a concrete architecture/scope concern grounded in the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: integerToBytes in AuthzClientCryptoProvider silently truncates R/S BigInteger values longer than qLength, enabling signature malleability and acceptance of non-canonically encoded signatures

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider#integerToBytes, when s.toByteArray() is longer than qLength it silently truncates the most-significant bytes (copies only the last qLength bytes) with no validation. This means oversized/non-canonically encoded ASN.1 INTEGER values for R/S (beyond the expected length) are not rejected and can be mapped to a different fixed-width value, which is incorrect for strict signature decoding and can enable multiple encodings to collapse to the same concatenated form.

adjudication_records.issue_text: detectProvider in CryptoIntegration replaces the fail-closed error on multiple CryptoProvider implementations with silent order-based precedence, allowing silent replacement of the crypto backend

adjudication.rationale: The diff verifiably changes behavior in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider`: it now loads all `CryptoProvider`s, sorts them by `CryptoProvider::order` descending, and always returns the first provider. The previous hard-fail on `foundProviders.size() > 1` was removed, and additional providers are only mentioned via `logger.debugf("Ignored crypto providers: ...")`. This does enable precedence-based selection instead of fail-closed behavior when multiple providers are on the classpath, which could allow an unintended/undesired provider to be chosen without a visible error (only debug logging). That’s a real review concern grounded in the diff, though it appears intentional to allow multiple providers to coexist (e.g., authz-client’s provider vs default).

adjudication_records.issue_text: CryptoProvider ties in order (all existing providers return 200) have no defined winner, resolved by classpath-dependent ServiceLoader iteration order

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to allow multiple CryptoProvider implementations and select one by sorting providers by CryptoProvider::order descending. However, all existing providers in this diff (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return the same order value (200), so the sort does not define a deterministic winner among them. With equal keys, the chosen provider is effectively whichever ServiceLoader iteration encounters first, which depends on classpath/service configuration order. This introduces non-deterministic provider selection where previously the code failed fast when multiple providers were present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ASN1Decoder readSequence length accounting loop can go negative without a check, accepting truncated and over-long TLVs instead of strict DER rejection
matched_golden_ids: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both comments flag a length-accounting bug where subtracting consumed bytes from the remaining length can drive the length negative and lead to incorrect parsing/acceptance of malformed encodings. The golden comment attributes the negative starting value to indefinite-length encoding (-1), while the candidate describes the same negative-length outcome and its consequences (truncated/over-long TLVs accepted).

adjudication_records.issue_text: concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains dead encoder writes (two discarded ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls) that execute BigInteger encoding twice with zero behavior effect

adjudication.rationale: In `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER(...)`, there are two standalone calls `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose results are discarded. They allocate an encoder, encode the BigInteger into its internal buffer, and then drop it, producing no externally observable effect because the returned byte arrays are never used. The actual returned value is built by a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(...), ...)` call, so the first two writes are redundant (unnecessary work/allocations), not a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ECDSAAlgorithmTest roundtrip assertion is encoder-vs-decoder self-consistency only, never verifying against original DER bytes or Signature.verify(), so encoding bugs pass undetected

adjudication.rationale: The new ECDSAAlgorithmTest only asserts internal round-trip consistency between AuthzClientCryptoProvider’s DER↔RS conversion helpers: it takes Signature.sign() DER bytes, converts to concatenated RS, converts back to DER, then converts back to RS and compares rsConcat vs rsConcat2. It never checks that the re-encoded DER (asn1Des) is valid for verification (e.g., Signature.verify with the public key) or matches the original DER output, so a paired-but-wrong encoder/decoder implementation could still make this test pass.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test exercises CryptoIntegration.init/AuthzClient provider loading path or detectProvider ordering; ECDSAAlgorithmTest instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly, so misregistered service files or order() collisions go undetected

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new SPI registration file (authz/client/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider) and changes provider selection logic to sort by CryptoProvider::order and pick the highest (common/.../CryptoIntegration.java). AuthzClient.create(...) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). However, the only added test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly and never exercises CryptoIntegration.init/ServiceLoader-based discovery or the new ordering/"ignored providers" behavior, so a misnamed/mispackaged service file or order() collision/regression would not be detected by tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Dead code in AuthzClientCryptoProvider: two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) results are created and discarded with zero behavioral effect

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, there are two standalone statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose results are not stored or used. The method later correctly builds the DER sequence via `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger))`, so the discarded encoders have no behavioral effect and are indeed dead/unnecessary code (extra allocations/calls).

adjudication_records.issue_text: CryptoIntegration.detectProvider behavior changed from throwing IllegalStateException on multiple providers to silently picking the highest-order provider and only logging ignored ones at debug level, potentially silently reclassifying which crypto implementation a deployed server uses (e.g., non-FIPS instead of FIPS or vice versa)

adjudication.rationale: The diff verifiably changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` from fail-fast (throwing `IllegalStateException` when `foundProviders.size() > 1`) to sorting providers by `CryptoProvider::order` (descending) and returning the first, while only logging ignored providers at `debug` level. This can indeed silently change which crypto provider is selected when multiple are present on the classpath. Additionally, the diff sets `order()` to `200` for `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider`, so ties are possible; with equal order values, the selected provider may depend on `ServiceLoader` iteration order, making selection potentially nondeterministic and harder to detect because it no longer throws.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK default KeyStore's provider rather than a BouncyCastle provider, contradicting the interface contract

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e., the JDK/default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider. This conflicts with the `CryptoProvider` interface intent (`Provider getBouncyCastleProvider();`) and differs from other implementations in the diff (`DefaultCryptoProvider`/`FIPS1402Provider` return actual BC providers; `WildFlyElytronProvider` returns `null`). Any caller expecting a BC provider from this method would get the wrong provider.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Most CryptoProvider methods in the new code throw UnsupportedOperationException

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (implements `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`), many required interface methods are stubbed out with `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")` (e.g., `getAlgorithmProvider`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getPemUtils`, `getKeyPairGen`, `getSignature`, etc.). This is directly verifiable in the diff. Whether it becomes a runtime bug depends on which `CryptoProvider` methods the authz-client (or its dependencies) actually call, which is not shown here; but it is a concrete, diff-grounded completeness/architecture concern for a provider that is registered via `META-INF/services/...CryptoProvider` and initialized in `AuthzClient.create()`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Removal of fail-fast check for multiple crypto providers (foundProviders.size() > 1) allows silent provider selection, and with equal order() values (200) between DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider the tie is resolved non-deterministically via ServiceLoader iteration order, with no INFO/WARN logging for visibility

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() from throwing on multiple CryptoProvider implementations to sorting by order() and silently selecting the first, only emitting DEBUG logs for ignored providers. However, multiple built-in providers in this diff all return the same order() value (200) (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider), so when more than one is present the selection is not uniquely determined by the new ordering and will fall back to ServiceLoader iteration order, which can vary by classpath/service file ordering. This is a behavior change from fail-fast to potentially non-deterministic provider choice without INFO/WARN visibility.

adjudication_records.issue_text: logger.debugf(builder.toString()) uses a dynamic string as format template with no arguments, causing UnknownFormatConversionException if a provider class name contains '%'; should be logger.debugf("%s", builder.toString())

adjudication.rationale: In common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java, the new code builds a message dynamically and calls `logger.debugf(builder.toString());`. `debugf` treats its first argument as a printf-style format string; if any ignored provider class name (appended into the StringBuilder) contains a '%' character, it will be interpreted as a format specifier and can throw a formatting exception at runtime when debug logging is enabled. Using `logger.debugf("%s", builder.toString())` (or `logger.debug(builder.toString())`) would avoid this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: getBouncyCastleProvider() in AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns the JVM's default KeyStore provider (e.g. SUN) instead of a BouncyCastle provider, causing NoSuchAlgorithmException or wrong-provider failures for callers; should throw UnsupportedOperationException or return an actual BC provider

adjudication.rationale: In the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns the provider backing the JVM’s default keystore type (commonly `SUN`), not a BouncyCastle provider. This contradicts the `CryptoProvider` interface contract (`Provider getBouncyCastleProvider();`) and can lead callers that expect an actual BC provider to select the wrong provider or fail when they try to use BC-specific algorithms/registrations. The issue is directly verifiable from the added method body in `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: integerToBytes silently truncates high-order bytes when the integer exceeds qLength bytes (copying only low bytes), producing structurally valid but cryptographically wrong signatures with no exception or log; should reject values that don't fit

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider#asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength) does truncate when s.toByteArray().length > qLength by copying only the low-order qLength bytes. That behavior is visible in the diff and would indeed silently discard high-order bytes for oversized ASN.1 INTEGERs. However, in the shown usage (DER produced by Java Signature.sign in the added test), r/s should be within the curve order and any extra byte is typically just a leading 0x00 for sign, where truncation is effectively harmless. The finding is thus a concrete, diff-grounded hardening/edge-case concern (reject non-fitting integers) rather than a clearly triggered defect in the code as introduced.

adjudication_records.issue_text: concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs and discards two throwaway ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) results on every invocation — dead code causing wasted allocation on a hot path and misleading readers

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, there are two standalone statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose results are not stored or used. The actual returned value is built by a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(...), ASN1Encoder.create().write(...))`. The two standalone calls are therefore dead code causing unnecessary allocations/IOExceptions handling overhead and reader confusion, but they do not change correctness because they have no side effects beyond allocation.
